## Compact evidence pack

### 1) Eating-disorder onset in adolescence — peer-reviewed
**Source page:** Tan, J. S. K., Tan, L. E. S., Davis, C., & Chew, C. S. E. (2022). “[Eating disorders in children and adolescents](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9329554/).” *Singapore Medical Journal, 63*(6), 294–298. https://doi.org/10.11622/smedj.2022078. PMCID: PMC9329554; PMID: 36043292.

**Exact quotation:** “Eating disorders commonly develop in adolescence, with conditions such as AN and BN having an average age of onset of 14 years.”

**Workshop-safe takeaway:** Adolescence is a meaningful period for onset and early identification, not a diagnosis or prediction for any individual. The quoted average is specifically framed by the authors for anorexia nervosa (AN) and bulimia nervosa (BN); do not present it as an age at which every eating disorder begins.

### 2) Brain development continues well beyond childhood
**Source page:** National Institute of Mental Health. (2023, revised). “[The Teen Brain: 7 Things to Know](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/the-teen-brain-7-things-to-know)” (NIH Publication No. 23-MH-8078).

**Exact quotation:** “The brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late 20s.”

The same NIMH page explains that the prefrontal cortex is among the last areas to mature and links it with planning, prioritising, and decision-making. This is a useful corrective to the misconception that brain development ends in childhood—while avoiding the equally misleading message that teenagers cannot make thoughtful choices.

### 3) Evolutionary influences on cognitive bias — peer-reviewed
**Source page:** Korteling, J. E. (Hans), Paradies, G. L., & Sassen-van Meer, J. P. (2023). “[Cognitive bias and how to improve sustainable decision making](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071311/).” *Frontiers in Psychology, 14*, Article 1129835. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1129835. PMCID: PMC10071311; PMID: 37026083.

**Exact quotation:** “Effects of the workings of our brain and of our evolutionary heritage on decision making manifest most prominently in cognitive biases.”

The article describes biases as systematic tendencies that can produce inaccurate or suboptimal judgments, while also noting that fast, heuristic thinking can be practical in time-pressured, information-limited conditions. That distinction is valuable for young people: biases are common human shortcuts, not personal defects. A careful workshop framing is that evolutionary accounts help explain *why* shortcuts may exist; they do **not** mean a bias is inevitable, morally bad, or an explanation for any one person’s eating or mental-health experience.

## Album tracks and discussion prompt

**Underlying track-list source:** Sony Music Vinyl, “[Lauryn Hill: *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* LP](https://vinyl.sonymusic.com/products/lauryn-hill-the-miseducation-of-lauryn-hill-lp).” The page lists, among others:

- “Lost Ones”
- “Ex-Factor”
- “To Zion”
- “Doo Wop (That Thing)”
- “Superstar”
- “Final Hour”
- “When It Hurts so Bad”
- “Forgive Them Father”
- “Everything Is Everything”
- “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill”

### Recommended prompt: **“Everything Is Everything”**
I would use **“Everything Is Everything”** because its title alone opens a non-clinical, non-stigmatising discussion of interconnected influences: body and brain changes, relationships, culture, stress, and the quick interpretations people make of themselves and others. It can connect all three evidence strands without implying that a song—or a young person’s distress—has one simple cause.

**Prompt:** *When we are under pressure, what influences the stories we tell ourselves about our bodies, worth, choices, or future? Which of those influences are immediate feelings or mental shortcuts, which come from other people and environments, and what could help us pause and choose a kinder, better-informed response?*

For safeguarding, invite discussion of messages and coping rather than personal weights, dieting behaviours, or disclosures; remind participants that concerns about eating or mental health deserve support from a trusted adult or health professional.

I’m assembling a short youth mental-health workshop and need a compact, citable evidence pack. Please locate credible sources on: (1) the typical adolescent onset of eating disorders—preferably a peer-reviewed article, with an exact quotation and full citation details; (2) continuing brain development beyond childhood; and (3) evolutionary influences on cognitive bias. I want the underlying source pages, not merely search-result summaries.

Also pull at least five track titles from *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* and identify one that would serve as a productive discussion prompt for adolescents in relation to those themes. Give me a concise synthesis with links, quotations where warranted, and your rationale for the song selection.

R1.reason: The agent opened the PMC article after a Google search and supplied a peer-reviewed Singapore Medical Journal citation plus the exact quote, “Eating disorders commonly develop in adolescence...”.

R2.reason: The NIMH source page was opened and correctly cited, but it was opened directly rather than from a Google result as required by the verification standard.

R3.reason: The agent opened the PMC article after searching Google and provided its title, journal publisher, DOI/URL, and an exact statement connecting evolutionary heritage to cognitive biases.

R4.reason: Separate eating-disorder, NIMH brain-development, and cognitive-bias source tabs were open, and the final brief coherently connected all three themes for adolescents.

R5.reason: Although the response lists more than five valid album tracks, it cites Sony Music Vinyl and no Wikipedia album page was opened.

R6.reason: “Everything Is Everything” is a valid album song and the rationale links the three themes, but the required Wikipedia track-list page was not opened for verification.

R7.reason: The response is a concise brief containing the three evidence sources, citations, quote, tracks, and rationale, but it fails the required Wikipedia sourcing/open-page condition for the album material.

P1_asked_for.reason: It supplies three credible linked source pages, exact quotations and citation details where requested, more than five album tracks, and a concise adolescent-focused rationale and prompt for the selected song.

P2_readable_for_them.reason: The answer is compact, formally written, appropriately qualified, and uses terminology that a highly educated, research-literate user could readily assess.

P3_actionable.reason: Direct links to the underlying PMC, NIMH, and Sony pages are provided alongside reusable quotations, bibliographic details, and a ready-to-use discussion prompt.

P4_gap_handling.reason: It appropriately handles the unstated safeguarding risk of a youth mental-health workshop by recommending non-stigmatising framing and avoiding prompts that solicit potentially harmful personal disclosures.

P5_overall.reason: The response delivers a citable, usable workshop evidence pack with the requested cultural discussion component and sensible youth-focused caveats.
